title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about reflecting on experience: how to turn a practice or work-based experience into learning you can name and use. By the end you will be able to explain experiential learning and Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, use the cycle to structure a reflection, and articulate what you learned in a way that meets how this learning is assessed.

You have already met practice- and work-based learning and worked at making the most of it. This course takes the final step: reflection. Reflection is what turns an experience you had into a graduate who can say what they now know and will do differently.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain experiential learning and how Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle structures learning from experience
use Kolb's cycle to structure a reflection on a practice or work-based experience
articulate what you learned from an experience in a way that meets how it is assessed.

title: In real academic practice
body: Reflection is the habit professional work runs on. Appraisals, placements, clinical supervision, teaching portfolios and chartership all ask you to look back at what you did, work out what it taught you, and act differently next time. Build a disciplined way of reflecting now and it carries into every placement of your degree and into professional practice beyond it.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, learning through experience: what experiential learning is and the four modes of Kolb's cycle. Second, reflecting through the cycle: using those modes to structure a reflection, worked through a real example. Third, articulating what you learned: how this learning is assessed and how to evidence it. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can explain experiential learning and how Kolb's cycle structures learning from experience.
I can use Kolb's cycle to structure a reflection on a practice or work-based experience.

title: Orientation
body: You have done the experience; now comes the part that turns it into learning. Experiential learning is the idea that you learn by doing and then making sense of what you did. This lesson looks at that idea and at the model most used to describe it, David Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, so that reflection becomes something you understand rather than something you are simply told to do.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to work with a model, not just recognise one. The aim is to understand experiential learning well enough to explain it to someone else, and to hold the four modes of Kolb's cycle, and the two dimensions beneath them, clearly enough to use them in the lessons that follow.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain experiential learning as the creation of knowledge through the transformation of experience
describe the four modes of Kolb's cycle: experiencing, reflecting, thinking and acting
explain how grasping and transforming experience relate the four modes when you learn from an experience in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Experiential learning is learning through experience. Its best-known statement comes from David Kolb, who defined learning as the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience. The experience alone is not the learning; the learning is what you do with it afterwards.

Kolb set this out as a cycle with four modes: experiencing (the concrete experience itself), reflecting (looking back at what happened and why), thinking (making sense of it against ideas and theory), and acting (trying out what you have worked out). Two dimensions sit beneath these modes. You grasp experience either by living it directly or by thinking about it in the abstract, and you transform experience either by reflecting on it or by actively experimenting. The four modes are where those two dimensions meet.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent experience on your course or in work. Which of Kolb's four modes did you naturally reach, and which did you skip? What would it take to complete the cycle?

title: Summary
body: Experiential learning is the creation of knowledge through the transformation of experience: the event alone is not the learning. Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle names four modes, experiencing, reflecting, thinking and acting, and two dimensions beneath them, grasping and transforming experience. You can now explain the idea and describe the cycle. The next lesson puts the cycle to work, using it to structure a reflection on a real experience.

_items.title: See pages 225 to 226 of Chapter 12, 'Learning by Doing - Practice- and Work-Based Learning', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you met Kolb's cycle as a model. This lesson puts it to work. Knowing the four modes is one thing; using them to structure a real reflection, so that an experience actually yields learning, is another. We will work through a full example and then set out how you do the same with your own experience.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not just following the cycle but handling it with judgement. That means seeing what each stage contributes, noticing when a reflection has skipped one, and understanding why the cycle is a way of thinking rather than a form to fill in once, in a fixed order.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use Kolb's four modes to structure a reflection on a practice or work-based experience
analyse a worked reflection to see what each stage of the cycle contributes
explain why the cycle is a model to think with rather than a fixed one-way sequence when you reflect on work in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
To reflect through the cycle, you take one real experience and move it through the four modes in turn. You set out what happened (experiencing), look back at what you noticed and why (reflecting), make sense of it against ideas you have met (thinking), and decide what you will do differently (acting). Each mode does a job the others cannot.

The order helps, but it is not a rule. Kolb's cycle is a model to think with, not a sequence that must always run once, in one direction. You might loop back to look again at what happened, or jump ahead to test an idea and return. Reading the cycle as a fixed one-way sequence is a well-known way to misuse it. What matters is that every mode is reached, not that they are reached in a rigid order.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of an experience you could reflect on. Which mode do you tend to linger in, and which do you rush or skip? What would a more balanced pass through the cycle change?

title: Summary
body: Reflecting through the cycle means taking one real experience and moving it through all four modes: setting out what happened, reflecting on why, thinking it through against ideas, and deciding what to do differently. The order helps but is not a rule; the cycle is a model to think with, and what matters is that every mode is reached. You can now structure a reflection and see what each stage contributes. The last lesson turns that reflection into an account that meets how this learning is assessed.

_items.title: See pages 225 to 229 of Chapter 12, 'Learning by Doing - Practice- and Work-Based Learning', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You can now reflect through the cycle. This lesson is about showing it. Practice- and work-based learning is usually assessed not on the experience itself but on the account you give of what you learned from it. This lesson looks at how that assessment works and at how to articulate your learning so that the insight is visible to a reader.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to produce and judge reflective accounts, not just write them. The aim is to understand what assessors are looking for, to articulate your own learning so it reads as evidenced insight rather than description, and to tell a strong reflective account from a weak one.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how practice- and work-based learning is assessed, and why reflection sits at its centre
articulate what you learned from an experience as an evidenced reflective account
judge whether a reflective account in {{context}} shows the insight assessors look for.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Practice- and work-based learning is hard to assess with a standard mark scheme, because each workplace has its own culture and its own uncertainty. So assessment usually turns on reflection: tutors ask you to show, in a reflective account, what you gained from the experience and how you made sense of it. The experience is the occasion; your articulated learning is what is actually marked.

A strong account does more than describe. It shows honest reflection on what happened, including what did not go well, connects the experience to ideas or professional standards, and draws out specific, evidenced insight into your own performance and the setting you worked in. A weak account retells events or lists feelings. Articulating your learning well means making the insight visible, with enough of the experience shown for a reader to trust it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you would evidence your learning from a recent experience to someone assessing it. What insight could you show, and what is the risk that your account slips back into description?

title: Summary
body: Practice- and work-based learning is assessed through reflection because each workplace differs: what is marked is the learning you articulate, not the experience itself. A strong reflective account moves beyond description to evidenced insight, honest reflection, a link to ideas or standards, and a specific change you will make. You can now explain how this learning is assessed, articulate your own learning, and judge an account against what assessors look for. With the model, the method and the articulation in place, you can turn any experience into learning you can show.

_items.title: See pages 224 to 230 of Chapter 12, 'Learning by Doing - Practice- and Work-Based Learning', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Reflecting on experience is no longer a vague instruction: it is something you can do with a method. You can explain experiential learning and Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, with its four modes and the two dimensions of grasping and transforming experience. You can use the cycle to structure a reflection, reaching every mode rather than following a rigid order. And you can articulate what you learned in a way that meets how this learning is assessed. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, reflecting on experience is something you practise throughout your degree and beyond. Every placement review, every portfolio, every appraisal and every professional body that asks for reflective practice draws on the same method you have built here. The ability to take an experience, work out what it taught you, and act differently is what turns time spent into genuine development.

_items.title: See pages 220 to 230 of Chapter 12, 'Learning by Doing - Practice- and Work-Based Learning', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Kolb's four modes
body: Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle moves through four modes. Reveal each one to see what it involves and how it leads to the next.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Experiencing
_items.body: You take part in the experience itself: the placement, the lesson, the shift, the project. This is concrete experience, lived directly rather than read about.

_items.title: Reflecting
_items.body: You look back at what happened and why. What did you notice, what surprised you, how did it feel, and what went as planned or did not?

_items.title: Thinking
_items.body: You make sense of the experience against ideas and theory. You move from the single event to a more general understanding you can carry to other situations.

_items.title: Acting
_items.body: You try out what you have worked out. The next experience tests it, and the cycle begins again, now informed by what you learned.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students finish the same first-year placement and are asked what they learned from it.

{{learner-a}} says the placement was useful and that they enjoyed it and gained experience. That is a report of the experience, not learning from it. {{learner-a}} has stopped at the experiencing mode: the event happened, but it has not been reflected on, thought through, or turned into anything to carry forward. The experience sits as a memory, not as knowledge.

{{learner-b}} says the placement showed them that they manage a group better when they plan the opening few minutes carefully. One session that drifted at the start was hard to recover. They noticed what happened, worked out why, drew a general lesson, and named what they will do differently. {{learner-b}} has moved through the whole cycle, transforming the experience into knowledge.

Both students had the same placement. Only {{learner-b}} transformed it, which is what experiential learning means.

title: Reflecting through the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these prompts to move an experience through all four modes, rather than stopping at the first.
instruction: Tick each item once you have worked through it.

_items.text: Experiencing: have I set out what actually happened, concretely, before judging it?
Reflecting: have I asked what I noticed, what surprised me, and what went well or did not?
Thinking: have I linked the experience to an idea or theory that explains it?
Thinking: have I drawn a general lesson that would apply beyond this one event?
Acting: have I named something specific I will do differently next time?
Have I avoided stopping at 'it was useful' without saying what I learned?

title: Formative check: what experiential learning means
displayTitle: Which statement best captures what experiential learning means?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best captures what experiential learning means?

_items.text: That knowledge is created by transforming experience, not by the experience alone.
_items.feedback: Yes. The learning is what you do with the experience, not the experience by itself.

_items.text: That you learn best from hands-on tasks rather than from reading.
_items.feedback: That is a claim about study styles, not what experiential learning means.

_items.text: That any experience teaches you something as long as you pay attention.
_items.feedback: Attention is not enough; the experience has to be transformed through the cycle.

_items.text: That practical work matters more than theory at university.
_items.feedback: Experiential learning is not a ranking of practice over theory; it is how experience becomes knowledge.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Knowledge is created by transforming experience, not by the experience alone.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about transforming an experience, not just having one.
_incorrect.final: Experiential learning means knowledge is created by transforming experience. The other options confuse it with study styles, attention, or ranking practice over theory.

title: Formative check: the four modes
displayTitle: Kolb's cycle moves through four modes. Which option lists them in the order this lesson gave?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option lists Kolb's four modes in order?

_items.text: Experiencing, reflecting, thinking, acting.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the order the lesson set out.

_items.text: Thinking, experiencing, acting, reflecting.
_items.feedback: These are the right modes but not in the order given.

_items.text: Reflecting, acting, experiencing, thinking.
_items.feedback: These are the right modes but not in the order given.

_items.text: Planning, doing, checking, repeating.
_items.feedback: These are not the modes of Kolb's cycle.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The four modes are experiencing, reflecting, thinking and acting.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Recall the mode you start from, the concrete experience itself.
_incorrect.final: The four modes are experiencing, reflecting, thinking and acting. One option reorders them and one names a different model.

title: Formative check: transforming an experience
displayTitle: You have just had a concrete experience in {{context}}. In Kolb's terms, which move transforms it into learning?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move transforms a concrete experience into learning?

_items.text: Reflecting on it, then thinking it through against ideas, before acting differently.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflection and thinking transform the experience into learning you can use in {{context}}.

_items.text: Repeating the same task until it feels familiar.
_items.feedback: Repetition builds habit, but it does not transform the experience through the cycle.

_items.text: Writing down exactly what happened and leaving it there.
_items.feedback: A record of events is the experiencing mode only; nothing has been transformed.

_items.text: Moving straight to the next experience without pausing.
_items.feedback: Without reflecting and thinking, the experience is not transformed into learning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflecting and then thinking an experience through is how it is transformed into learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which moves take you beyond simply having or recording the experience?
_incorrect.final: An experience is transformed by reflecting on it and thinking it through, then acting. Repeating, recording or rushing on leaves it untransformed.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Four questions, one experience
body: The four modes become four questions you put to a single experience. Reveal each to see what it asks and the work it does.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Experiencing: what actually happened?
_items.body: Set the scene plainly before you judge it. What did you do, who was involved, what was the task? A clear account of the experience is the ground everything else stands on.

_items.title: Reflecting: what did I notice, and why?
_items.body: Look back at the experience and your part in it. What went well, what did not, how did it feel, what surprised you? This is where honest noticing happens, including the uncomfortable parts.

_items.title: Thinking: what does it mean?
_items.body: Move from the single event to a general understanding. Link what happened to an idea or theory, and work out a lesson that would hold in other situations, not just this one.

_items.title: Acting: what will I do differently?
_items.body: Turn the lesson into a specific next step you can test. Without this mode the reflection stays an interesting thought; with it, the experience changes what you do.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students each have a seminar presentation that goes badly, and each writes a reflection on it.

{{learner-a}} writes that the presentation went poorly, that they felt nervous, and that they will try to do better next time. Every sentence is about feeling, and the one lesson is vague. The reflection stops between experiencing and reflecting: there is no thinking that explains why it went badly, and 'do better' names no action. Nothing has been transformed.

{{learner-b}} sets out what happened: they over-ran and lost the audience. They reflect on why: they had written too many slides and read straight from them. They think it through, linking it to a point from their communication module, that an audience follows a spoken argument, not dense slides. Then they act: next time they will cut to three slides and speak to notes. The reflection moves through all four modes, so the setback becomes a usable lesson.

Both students had the same difficult experience. Only {{learner-b}} took it round the cycle, which is what turned it into learning.

title: Structuring your reflection
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these checks on a reflection you are writing to make sure it moves through the whole cycle.
instruction: Tick each item once your reflection does it.

_items.text: Have I described what actually happened before I started judging it?
Have I reflected honestly, including on what did not go well?
Have I linked the experience to an idea or theory, not just my feelings?
Have I drawn a lesson that would apply beyond this one event?
Have I named a specific action I will take next time?
Have I checked that no mode is missing, without forcing a rigid order?

title: Formative check: a complete reflection
displayTitle: You are reflecting on an experience using Kolb's cycle. Which of these is the clearest sign your reflection is complete?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the clearest sign a reflection through the cycle is complete?

_items.text: It reaches all four modes, ending with a specific action you will take.
_items.feedback: Yes. A complete reflection reaches every mode and ends in action.

_items.text: It describes what happened in careful detail.
_items.feedback: Detailed description is only the experiencing mode; it is not a complete reflection.

_items.text: It explains how the experience made you feel.
_items.feedback: Feelings belong to reflecting, but on their own they do not complete the cycle.

_items.text: It is written strictly in the order experiencing, reflecting, thinking, acting.
_items.feedback: A fixed order is not the test; reaching every mode is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A complete reflection reaches all four modes and ends with an action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reflection needs beyond describing or feeling.
_incorrect.final: A reflection is complete when it reaches all four modes and ends in a specific action. Detail, feeling, or a rigid order are not the test.

title: Formative check: analysing the worked reflection
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do that the first did not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do that the first did not?

_items.text: Thought the experience through against an idea and named a specific action.
_items.feedback: Yes. Thinking and acting are the modes the first student never reached.

_items.text: Described the experience in more detail.
_items.feedback: The difference was not detail; it was reaching the thinking and acting modes.

_items.text: Admitted to feeling nervous about it.
_items.feedback: Both students noted feelings; that was not what made the difference.

_items.text: Wrote the reflection in the correct fixed order.
_items.feedback: A fixed order was not the point; reaching every mode was.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student reached the thinking and acting modes, which the first did not.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the modes the first student's reflection never reached.
_incorrect.final: The second student thought the experience through and named an action, reaching the thinking and acting modes. More detail, feelings, or a fixed order were not the difference.

title: Formative check: the cycle is not a fixed sequence
displayTitle: While reflecting on an experience in {{context}}, you loop back to re-examine what happened before settling an idea. What does this tell you about Kolb's cycle?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does looping back tell you about Kolb's cycle?

_items.text: The cycle is a model to think with; reaching every mode matters more than a fixed order.
_items.feedback: Yes. Looping back is fine, because the cycle is a model, not a one-way sequence.

_items.text: You are using the cycle wrongly and should restart in the correct order.
_items.feedback: No single order is correct; reaching every mode is what matters.

_items.text: You should skip the thinking mode to save time.
_items.feedback: Skipping a mode weakens the reflection; that is the opposite of the point.

_items.text: The cycle only works if each mode is done exactly once.
_items.feedback: The cycle allows looping; a mode can be revisited.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The cycle is a model to think with, so looping back is part of using it well.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Recall what the lesson said about the cycle being a model rather than a rigid order.
_incorrect.final: Looping back shows the cycle is a model to think with, not a one-way sequence. What matters is reaching every mode, in whatever order serves the reflection.

definition: A written account in which you set out what you learned from an experience and how, rather than simply what happened.
extendedDefinition: In practice- and work-based learning, the reflective account is usually what is assessed. It is expected to move beyond description to evidenced insight: honest reflection, a link to ideas or professional standards, and specific lessons about your own performance and the setting.
example: A reflective account on a placement does not just report the tasks done; it explains what they revealed about how the student works and what they will change.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students submit a reflective account of the same work placement.

{{learner-a}} writes a clear, orderly account of what the placement involved: the team, the daily tasks, the project they helped on. It reads well and is accurate. But it is a description. It tells the assessor what happened and little about what {{learner-a}} learned, so there is almost nothing to credit as reflection or insight.

{{learner-b}} writes less about the tasks and more about what they revealed. They describe one moment a plan failed, reflect on their part in it, link it to a professional standard they had read about, and set out what they now do differently and why. The account shows evidenced insight into their own performance. That is what the criteria reward.

Both students did the same placement and wrote to the same length. Only {{learner-b}} articulated the learning, which is what is actually assessed.

title: Writing an account that is assessed well
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these checks before you submit a reflective account, so the insight is visible to the assessor.
instruction: Tick each item once your account does it.

_items.text: Have I shown enough of what happened for the reader to follow, without retelling everything?
Have I reflected honestly, including on what did not go well?
Have I linked the experience to an idea, theory or professional standard?
Have I drawn specific insight about my own performance, not general remarks?
Have I said what I will do differently, with a reason?
Would a reader see learning here, rather than a description of events?

title: Formative check: why reflection is assessed
displayTitle: Why is practice- and work-based learning usually assessed through reflection rather than a standard mark scheme?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is this learning usually assessed through reflection?

_items.text: Because each workplace differs, so what is assessed is the learning you draw from it, not a fixed output.
_items.feedback: Yes. Standardised criteria are hard to apply across different workplaces, so the learning is what is assessed.

_items.text: Because reflection is easier for tutors to mark quickly.
_items.feedback: Reflective accounts are not quicker to mark; that is not the reason.

_items.text: Because the experience itself cannot be graded at all.
_items.feedback: The issue is the variety of workplaces, not that experience can never be graded.

_items.text: Because students prefer writing reflections to sitting exams.
_items.feedback: Student preference is not why reflection is used for assessment.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Because workplaces differ, assessment turns on the learning you articulate, not a fixed output.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about why a standard mark scheme is hard to apply across different workplaces.
_incorrect.final: Workplaces differ in culture and uncertainty, so what is assessed is the learning you draw from the experience, not a standard output.

title: Formative check: strong versus weak account
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second account stronger than the first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second reflective account stronger?

_items.text: It showed evidenced insight into the student's own learning, not just a description of events.
_items.feedback: Yes. Evidenced insight is what the criteria reward.

_items.text: It described the placement in more detail.
_items.feedback: More description does not make a stronger reflective account.

_items.text: It was written more clearly and was better organised.
_items.feedback: The first account also read well; clarity was not the difference.

_items.text: It was longer than the first account.
_items.feedback: Both wrote to the same length; length was not the difference.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second account showed evidenced insight into the student's own learning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second account showed beyond a description of events.
_incorrect.final: The second account was stronger because it showed evidenced insight into the student's learning. Detail, clarity and length were not the difference.

title: Formative check: judging an account
displayTitle: You are judging a reflective account of an experience in {{context}}. Which feature best shows the insight assessors look for?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which feature best shows the insight assessors look for?

_items.text: It links a specific moment to a lesson about the writer's own performance and names a change.
_items.feedback: Yes. Specific, evidenced insight that leads to a change is what assessors reward in {{context}}.

_items.text: It gives a complete, orderly description of everything that happened.
_items.feedback: A full description is not insight; it tells the reader events, not learning.

_items.text: It lists the writer's feelings at each stage of the placement.
_items.feedback: Feelings alone are not the evidenced insight assessors look for.

_items.text: It uses the correct reflective headings in a fixed order.
_items.feedback: Headings and order do not themselves show insight.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Linking a specific moment to a lesson about your own performance, and a change, shows real insight.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the feature that shows learning about the writer, not a description or a format.
_incorrect.final: Insight shows when a specific moment is linked to a lesson about the writer's performance and a change. Description, feelings or headings do not show it on their own.

body: Which statement best captures what experiential learning means, in Kolb's terms?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best captures what experiential learning means?

_items.text: Knowledge is created through the transformation of experience.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is Kolb's definition.

_items.text: Learning happens automatically whenever you do something practical.
_items.feedback: Doing something does not transform it into learning on its own.

_items.text: Hands-on work is more valuable than theory.
_items.feedback: Experiential learning is not a ranking of practice over theory.

_items.text: Experience is worth more than reading.
_items.feedback: It is about transforming experience, not ranking it against reading.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Knowledge is created through the transformation of experience.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what has to happen to an experience for it to become learning.

body: Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle has four modes. Which option names them?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which option names the four modes of Kolb's cycle?

_items.text: Experiencing, reflecting, thinking, acting.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those are the four modes.

_items.text: Planning, doing, checking, repeating.
_items.feedback: That is a different model, not Kolb's four modes.

_items.text: Reading, watching, practising, testing.
_items.feedback: These are not the modes of Kolb's cycle.

_items.text: Describing, feeling, concluding, forgetting.
_items.feedback: These are not Kolb's modes.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The four modes are experiencing, reflecting, thinking and acting.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Recall the four modes the course set out.

body: You are using Kolb's cycle to reflect on an experience. Which approach fits how the cycle is meant to be used?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach fits how Kolb's cycle is meant to be used?

_items.text: Make sure you reach every mode, looping back if you need to, rather than following a fixed order once.
_items.feedback: Yes. The cycle is a model to think with; reaching every mode is what matters.

_items.text: Run through the four modes once, strictly in order, and never revisit a stage.
_items.feedback: A fixed one-way order misuses the cycle.

_items.text: Choose the one mode that suits you and stay with it.
_items.feedback: A reflection needs every mode, not just one.

_items.text: Start with acting and stop once you have a plan.
_items.feedback: Acting without the earlier modes is not a full reflection.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reach every mode, looping back as needed, rather than following a rigid order.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Recall that the cycle is a model to think with, not a one-way sequence.

body: A student's reflection describes what happened and how they felt, but goes no further. Which modes of the cycle has the reflection reached?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which modes has a reflection that only describes and states feelings reached?

_items.text: Experiencing and the start of reflecting, but not thinking or acting.
_items.feedback: Yes. Describing and feeling do not reach thinking or acting.

_items.text: All four modes.
_items.feedback: Thinking and acting are missing.

_items.text: Thinking and acting only.
_items.feedback: These are the modes that are missing, not the ones reached.

_items.text: None of the modes.
_items.feedback: Describing the experience and noting feelings does reach the first modes.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Describing and feeling reach only experiencing and the start of reflecting.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which modes require making sense of the experience and acting on it?

body: Why is practice- and work-based learning usually assessed through a reflective account?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is this learning usually assessed through a reflective account?

_items.text: Because workplaces differ, so the learning you articulate is assessed rather than a standard output.
_items.feedback: Yes. The learning you articulate is what is marked.

_items.text: Because reflective accounts are quicker to mark.
_items.feedback: Speed of marking is not the reason.

_items.text: Because the work itself is never seen by tutors.
_items.feedback: The reason is the variety of workplaces, not that work is unseen.

_items.text: Because reflection avoids the need for any criteria.
_items.feedback: Criteria still apply; they reward evidenced insight.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Because workplaces differ, the learning you articulate is what is assessed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about why a standard output is hard to mark across different workplaces.

body: Which feature most clearly marks a strong reflective account rather than a weak one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which feature most clearly marks a strong reflective account?

_items.text: Evidenced insight into your own learning and a specific change you will make.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is what the criteria reward.

_items.text: A full, orderly description of everything that happened.
_items.feedback: Description is not insight.

_items.text: A list of the feelings you had during the experience.
_items.feedback: Feelings alone are not evidenced insight.

_items.text: Greater length than other students' accounts.
_items.feedback: Length does not make an account strong.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Evidenced insight into your learning, with a specific change, marks a strong account.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the feature that shows learning, not description, feelings or length.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what experiential learning is and the model that describes it, how to structure a reflection through Kolb's cycle, and how to articulate what you learned so it can be assessed. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a perfect reflective routine. The aim is to see reflection as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it carries on past this course and into every placement and module that follows.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together experiential learning, structured reflection and articulated learning as one continuing practice
recognise reflective practice at work in a student's ongoing experience and study
plan how you will keep reflecting on experience across your {{context}} studies and future placements

title: Concept: definition
body: Reflective practice is the three strands working as one habit. You take an experience and run it through Kolb's cycle, reaching every mode rather than stopping early. You reflect honestly, including on what did not go well, and you articulate what you learned so a reader can see the insight. Understanding the model, using it and articulating the result are not three tasks but one practice you repeat on each new experience.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, reflective practice runs across a whole degree, not once at the end of a single placement. After each experience you take it through the cycle, reflect honestly, and write down what you learned and will change. A short, honest round after each experience, with one change carried forward, is worth more than a long reflection written only when it is asked for.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of one kind of experience in your studies you could reflect on more regularly, such as a placement, a seminar or a piece of group work. When in your week would you run the cycle on it, and what would you write down?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Reflecting on experience is most useful when it becomes one continuing practice. You run the cycle on each experience, reflect honestly, and articulate what you learned, again and again across your studies. It is the habit, not any single account, that turns experience into learning you can show.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Understanding the model, using it and articulating the result are not three tasks but one habit you repeat on each experience. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Describe
_items.body: Set out what happened in the experience, honestly and in enough detail.

_items.title: Reflect
_items.body: Reflect on why it went that way, looking at what went well and what did not.

_items.title: Theorise
_items.body: Think it through against ideas or professional standards, then decide what to do differently.

_items.title: Articulate
_items.body: Articulate what you learned as an evidenced account, and carry the change into your next experience. The cycle turns again.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students each complete the same placement. One writes a tidy description of what the placement involved and leaves it there, treating the account as a one-off task. The other takes the experience through the cycle, reflects honestly on a moment that went wrong, links it to an idea from their course, and sets out what they will do differently next time. Over the year, the second student's accounts grow sharper, because reflection became a practice rather than a one-off.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep reflecting on experience
body: Use these to run reflection as a habit on each experience, rather than treating every placement as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I take the experience through every mode of the cycle, not stop at what happened?
Did I reflect honestly, including on what did not go well?
Did I connect the experience to ideas or professional standards?
Did I articulate a specific, evidenced change rather than only describe events?
Did I carry that change into my next experience?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat the model, the method and articulating your learning as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
body: Why is it more useful to treat the model, the method and articulating your learning as one practice rather than three separate tasks?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat the model, the method and articulating your learning as one practice rather than three separate tasks?

_items.text: Because each part feeds the next: the model tells you what to reach, the method reaches it, and articulating it shows the learning you can then build on.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three parts are one connected practice, each making the next possible.

_items.text: Because understanding the cycle on its own is enough to turn any experience into learning.
_items.feedback: Understanding the model is only the first part. It has to be used and articulated.

_items.text: Because treating them separately means you never have to look at what went wrong.
_items.feedback: Honest reflection still looks at what went wrong. That does not change when the parts join up.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less thought than working through three stages.
_items.feedback: It is not about less thought. One practice joins the stages so they reinforce each other.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The model, the method and the articulation form one practice, each part feeding the next.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how the three parts depend on and feed one another.

displayTitle: A student finishes a placement, takes it through Kolb's cycle, reflects honestly on a session that went wrong, and writes an account showing what they now do differently. What does this show?
body: A student finishes a placement, takes it through Kolb's cycle, reflects honestly on a session that went wrong, and writes an account showing what they now do differently. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student finishes a placement, takes it through Kolb's cycle, reflects honestly on a session that went wrong, and writes an account showing what they now do differently. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three strands worked as one practice: the model, the reflection and the articulation together turned the placement into learning they can show.
_items.feedback: Yes. All three parts ran together on one experience, which is the whole practice.

_items.text: That only the parts of the placement that went wrong are worth reflecting on.
_items.feedback: Honest reflection covers what went well too, not only what went wrong.

_items.text: That the account is strong because it describes the placement in full detail.
_items.feedback: Description alone is not the point. The strength is the evidenced insight, not the detail of events.

_items.text: That the experience alone, once finished, counts as the learning.
_items.feedback: The experience is the occasion. The learning is what the student did with it through the practice.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The model, the method and the articulation ran together on one experience, which is the practice working as a whole.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what the student did with the placement, step by step.

displayTitle: You want to use this practice to turn your {{context}} placements into learning you can show this year. Which plan best keeps reflection going as one honest practice?
body: You want to use this practice to turn your {{context}} placements into learning you can show this year. Which plan best keeps reflection going as one honest practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this practice to turn your your subject placements into learning you can show this year. Which plan best keeps reflection going as one honest practice?

_items.text: After each experience, take it through the cycle, reflect honestly, decide one change, and write a short account of what you learned.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole practice, honestly, again and again.

_items.text: Wait until the end of the year, then reflect once on every placement at once.
_items.feedback: One reflection at the end cannot shape placements you have already finished.

_items.text: Reflect only on the placements that went badly, so you do not dwell on the good ones.
_items.feedback: Honest reflection looks at what went well too, not only what went wrong.

_items.text: Describe each placement in full, without deciding what to change.
_items.feedback: Description is not enough. The practice needs an evidenced change you carry forward.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Taking each experience through the cycle, deciding one change, and articulating it keeps the practice going honestly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan repeats the whole practice, honestly, on each experience.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What best describes reflective practice as this course has built it?
body: What best describes reflective practice as this course has built it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What best describes reflective practice as this course has built it?

_items.text: One continuing practice in which you run an experience through the cycle, reflect honestly, and articulate what you learned.
_items.feedback: Yes. The model, the method and the articulation are one repeated practice.

_items.text: A single reflective account written once, at the end of a placement.
_items.feedback: One account at the end is not the practice. It is repeated, across experiences.

_items.text: Understanding Kolb's four modes well enough to name them.
_items.feedback: Naming the modes is only the first strand. The practice also uses and articulates them.

_items.text: Describing an experience in enough detail for a reader to picture it.
_items.feedback: Description is not the practice. The practice turns the experience into evidenced learning.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Across a term, a student reflects on each placement in turn, carries one change forward each time, and their accounts get stronger. What does this show?
body: Across a term, a student reflects on each placement in turn, carries one change forward each time, and their accounts get stronger. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Across a term, a student reflects on each placement in turn, carries one change forward each time, and their accounts get stronger. What does this show?

_items.text: That reflective practice works as a continuing habit: each honest round feeds the next and the learning builds over time.
_items.feedback: Yes. It is the repeated practice, not any one reflection, that improves the work.

_items.text: That the first placement must have been marked too harshly.
_items.feedback: The point is not the mark. It is that repeated reflection improved the accounts.

_items.text: That reflection only helps students who already write strong accounts.
_items.feedback: It helped this student improve from wherever they started.

_items.text: That writing more about each placement is what made the accounts stronger.
_items.feedback: Length is not the cause. The honest, repeated reflection is.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
